backups.overview: Mount Lyall is a remote, seldom-climbed summit above the Agnes Creek and Swamp Creek drainages south of Stehekin, sitting near the boundary of the Stephen Mather Wilderness (North Cascades National Park) and the Glacier Peak Wilderness. It is reached by a long trail approach from the head of Lake Chelan; the peak itself is a short but genuinely exposed scramble, not a simple talus walk.
backups.beta: An off-trail scramble approached via the Swamp Creek drainage off the Agnes Creek/PCT corridor. From a Swamp Creek camp, travelers cross Swamp Creek, climb through brush and open basin to about 4,000', then work up scree and talus (with lingering snow possible) toward a roughly 7,300' notch on the southwest ridge. From the notch, a traverse below a prominent white vertical rock band on grassy ledges leads to an exposed, narrowing class 3 gully; the final ~200' to the summit climbs through loose, stacked boulders (choss).
backups.turnaround: Turn back before committing to the exposed class 3 gully and choss near the summit if weather is deteriorating or the rock is wet — the loose, unroped terrain is significantly more hazardous to downclimb in poor visibility or rain, and the long brushy off-trail approach/return needs to be completed in daylight.
backups.permit: Free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit at the trailhead; no quota. No trailhead parking pass applies here, since the trailhead is reached by boat and shuttle rather than by car.
backups.comms: No cell service should be expected in this section of the Glacier Peak Wilderness; the area is reached only by boat/shuttle via Lake Chelan.

backups.pro_needs: No fixed protection or roped climbing is documented on this route; it is typically done as an unroped scramble, though a helmet is recommended given the loose rock (choss) in the summit gully and boulder field.
backups.approach: Via passenger ferry or floatplane from Chelan to Stehekin, then the PCT/Stehekin Valley Road to High Bridge; follow the Agnes Creek Trail and Swamp Creek drainage to Lyall's west basin. Roughly 35-40 miles round trip from High Bridge, so most parties camp en route. From the west basin, climb talus and heather to gain the southwest ridge, passing below a distinctive band of white rock; the route narrows into an exposed Class 3 gully near the summit, finishing over stacked Class 3-4 boulders to the summit block.
backups.descent_text: Downclimb the Class 3-4 boulders and exposed gully back into the west basin, then reverse the southwest ridge and basin descent to Swamp Creek and the Agnes Creek Trail.
backups.bail: Retreat is straightforward along the ascent line: downclimb the scree/talus below the 7,300' notch back into the open basin rather than continuing through the exposed gully above.

approach_variants.name: Agnes Creek and the Swamp Creek drainage to the west basin
approach_variants.notes: No road reaches this valley: take the passenger ferry or a floatplane up the lake, then the valley road or the shuttle to the bridge at the road end, and plan the trip around those timetables. Follow the crest trail south along Agnes Creek and work into the Swamp Creek drainage, which is a long way in — most parties camp en route rather than pushing through. From the drainage, climb through brush and open basin and then up scree and talus, with lingering snow possible, into the broad basin that sits below the peak on its west side. From that basin the climbing line turns south along the edge of a steep, larch-dotted scree slope and makes for the notch on the southwest ridge described below.
approach_variants.season: Midsummer into early autumn, and tied to the boat and shuttle timetable at both ends. Snow can linger on the talus below the notch.
hazards: A long, committing approach with no maintained trail through the upper drainage
Lingering snow on the talus below the notch
The southwest ridge cliffs out if taken directly — the line has to drop and traverse round a buttress
Sloping slabs with loose small rock on the traverse below the overhang
The final stretch climbs through stacked, loose boulders
The jagged crest above is not the line and should not be followed
approach_variants.baseFinding: THE 7,300 FT NOTCH IS THE FIRST PROOF AND THE WHITE ROCK STRIP IS THE SECOND. From the broad basin below the peak, turn south along the edge of a steep scree slope dotted with larch and make a beeline through talus and snow for the notch on the southwest ridge at about 7,300 ft. That notch is the gateway; a gap without the scree-and-larch slope leading to it is the wrong one. From the notch, walking up the southwest ridge leads directly into cliffs — this is expected and is not a sign you are off route. The fix is to drop about a hundred feet on grass to get round a buttress, then traverse upward beneath a striking vertical strip of white rock, hugging the edge below an overhang and taking care on the small loose rock lying over sloping slabs. That white band is unmistakable and is the confirmation you are on the correct traverse. Above it, keep scrambling just below the ridgeline rather than following the jagged crest itself, and finish over stacked boulders to the summit block.

bivy.name: Swamp Creek Camp — the base for Needle Peak, Mount Lyall and Lyall Ridge
bivy.notes: About nine miles south of High Bridge on the Pacific Crest Trail and roughly three beyond Fivemile, this is the working base for NEEDLE PEAK, MOUNT LYALL at 7,892 ft and the ridge between them. The unmaintained Swamp Creek trail leaves the corridor here and climbs toward Needle Peak's north ridge; the ground above is class 3 and 4 scrambling with real exposure and a helmet is wanted, and the northeast ridge of DARK PEAK continues over to Lyall, so a party willing to spend the days can link several of these summits off one camp. Budget five days for the full set including the boat at both ends, and something close to forty miles of walking. THE APPROACH IS ALL OF THE DIFFICULTY. These are not hard climbs by North Cascades standards; they are remote, brushy and slow, and the price of admission is the boat, the shuttle, the mileage and a good deal of unpleasant bushwhacking once you leave the corridor. Nothing about this is a weekend. Cedar Camp further up the valley is the alternative if this one is taken; Hemlock Camp above it is unsafe from falling insect-killed timber and should be skipped.
bivy.water: Swamp Creek at the camp, reliable. THIS IS ALSO THE HAUL POINT. There is no water on the ridges above and parties putting a high camp on Lyall Ridge or the north ridge of Needle carry it up from here, which is the single biggest load consideration on these summits.
bivy.permit: Free North Cascades backcountry permit, booked through the federal recreation booking site or collected in person as a walk-up. Bear canisters not specifically required at this camp; store food properly regardless. Fires are not appropriate here and restrictions are usually in force anyway.
bivy.capacity: A small trail camp, one or two parties. Like everything on this corridor it is shared with through-hikers in high summer.

bivy.name: Purple Point and Harlequin — the landing camps, and the boat that decides the trip
bivy.notes: READ THIS BEFORE ANY OTHER SITE IN THE ZONE. Stehekin has no road to it. The only practical way in is the scheduled passenger boat up Lake Chelan from Chelan or Fields Point Landing, and the timetable, not your fitness, sets the shape of the trip. The slow boat takes roughly four hours each way and the express about two and a half; a typical summer sailing leaves Chelan mid-morning, reaches Stehekin around midday, and turns round after a layover of an hour or ninety minutes. That means a party arriving on the boat has half a day at most before the last sailing out, and a party finishing a climb has to be at the landing on the boat's schedule or spend another night. Book the boat and the permit together and treat the return sailing as a hard deadline. From the landing a valley shuttle runs eleven miles up to High Bridge, four times a day in each direction in season, and it is the second half of the same logistics problem — miss it and you are walking. Purple Point is where you sleep if the boat gets in too late to reach the upper valley, and Harlequin is where you sleep if you are heading for the Company Creek road in the morning. Neither serves a summit directly, and both are essential.
bivy.water: Purple Point has potable water and vault toilets. Harlequin has vault toilets, tables, fire rings and animal-resistant food lockers, with the Stehekin River alongside. Neither is a water problem.
bivy.permit: This is a two-jurisdiction valley and it matters. The landing and the lower road are in the Lake Chelan National Recreation Area; the upper valley and everything you climb from it are North Cascades National Park. A backcountry permit is required year round for every overnight in the park backcountry, and the valley campgrounds require a free permit as well. Permits are issued through the federal recreation booking site, with a lottery in early March, winners assigned booking dates through late March and April, and the general release at seven in the morning Pacific in late April. Roughly sixty percent of permits are reservable and forty percent held for walk-ups. THERE IS NO PERMIT OFFICE IN STEHEKIN — a walk-up permit has to be collected in person elsewhere in the park complex before you get on the boat, which is the trap that ends more trips here than weather. Bear canisters are not required at these particular camps but food must be stored in the lockers or hung; the valley has bears and they know the campgrounds. Purple Point was free for the 2026 season.
bivy.capacity: Purple Point has six walk-in tent sites about ten minutes on foot from the boat dock. Harlequin, four and a half miles up the valley road, has seven walk-in sites with shared parking. Both are first come, first served and both are small enough that a busy summer afternoon fills them.

bivy.name: High Bridge Camp — the shuttle terminus and the base for McGregor Mountain
bivy.notes: The bus stops here and the walking starts here, so almost every trip in this zone passes through it. Its own summit is MCGREGOR MOUNTAIN, whose trail leaves the valley road near the guard station a mile or so from the bridge and is one of the biggest sustained climbs in the state: about 7.7 miles and 6,400 ft of gain to within half a mile of the top, past Coon Lake in the first mile and then switchback after switchback with almost no relief. The last 1,100 ft to the summit is exposed scrambling rather than trail, and an ice axe is wanted while snow is still lying on it. Doing that in a day from High Bridge is a very long outing and most parties camp here the night before rather than trying to fit it around the boat. Water is the specific worry: the lake and Coon Creek are early on and the upper mountain has nothing. High Bridge is also the start of the Agnes Creek trail south and the Pacific Crest corridor, so it is where the Agnes, Needle, Lyall and Dark Peak trips begin as well. Bicycles are allowed on the valley road and some parties ride the fourteen miles up rather than wait for a shuttle.
bivy.water: The Stehekin River and Agnes Creek at the bridge, plus Coon Creek on the trail above. Reliable, and it is worth filling here because the McGregor trail is a long way between sources once it starts switchbacking.
bivy.permit: Free backcountry permit required through the federal recreation booking site, collected in person outside the valley. No fee for the camp itself. Food storage is required; bears work the road end hard. Fires only where rings exist and only when no restriction is in force — Stage restrictions are common on the east side by midsummer.
bivy.capacity: A small road-end camp with a handful of sites, plus Bullion and Dolly Varden further up the valley road at ten and thirteen miles with two sites each. All first come, first served, none reservable.

bivy.name: Fivemile Camp, Agnes Creek
bivy.notes: Five miles south of High Bridge on the Pacific Crest Trail through Agnes Gorge, this is the junction camp and the last comfortable night before things get serious. It is the departure point for AGNES MOUNTAIN — the West Fork Agnes Creek trail leaves here heading west, and it is the start of the standard approach to the 8,115 ft summit, first climbed in 1936 from this same drainage. It is also the first night for parties heading further up Agnes Creek toward DARK PEAK, which is usually described as a three-day trip built off this camp and the ground above it. The camp itself is unremarkable: deep valley forest at 2,200 ft, no views, mosquitoes early in the season, and the creek. What makes it matter is position. Anything you climb from here is thousands of feet above and mostly trackless, so the difference between sleeping at High Bridge and sleeping here is a full extra push tacked onto an already long day.
bivy.water: Reliable — Agnes Creek runs at the camp all season. Fill completely here if you are heading up the West Fork, because there is no camp, no trail and no certainty of anything above.
bivy.permit: Free North Cascades backcountry permit required, reserved through the federal recreation booking site or taken as a walk-up collected in person before you reach the valley. Bear canisters are not on the required list for this camp, but food must be hung or stored properly and this is a long-established camp in bear country. No fires above the valley floor rings; check what restriction is running.
bivy.capacity: A modest forested camp on the creek, a couple of parties at most. It sees Pacific Crest Trail traffic through the summer, so it is busier in late July and August than its remoteness suggests.

backups.overview: The Southeast Ridge of Argonaut gives a longer and slightly more technical line to the summit than the northeast ridge, climbing the rocky crest over a series of steps and towers on excellent Stuart Range granite. With sustained moderate climbing, real exposure, and a remote setting, it rewards parties willing to make the long approach into this quieter corner of the range. Route-finding among the towers is part of the challenge and the fun.
backups.beta: From Colchuck Col, ascend the east ridge featuring blocky, generally solid but not sustained Class 4 to 5.6 climbing. The east faces of towers are typically easier than west sides, making cliff-out less likely if staying near the crest. Multiple pitch sections with good protection opportunities.
backups.turnaround: With the long approach and a multi-step ridge, fix a turnaround in the early afternoon. If you are behind schedule among the towers, the safest decision is often to rappel and retreat rather than push into deteriorating weather.
backups.rappels: Two single-rope rappels, or one double-rope rappel, back into the notch

backups.detailed_rack: Single set of nuts and cams from finger-size through ~3in covers the ridge's crack and corner systems; nothing larger is reported as needed. Rappel anchors are natural (slung horns, blocks, small trees), so bring cordelette/webbing to back up or replace tat if worn.

backups.pro_needs: Protection is moderate and intermittent on 4th-to-low-5th ridge terrain; parties report finding rappel anchors along the ridge as hoped, implying stations are already equipped and spaced for single-strand rope lengths. A distinct winter/mixed variant (East Ridge to a crossover into the NE Couloir) exists and is far more serious, requiring rock pro placed to protect wind-slab traverses plus ice tools/crampons — that is NOT the standard 5.6 summer rock route and should not be conflated with it.
backups.approach: Start at the Beverly Turnpike Trailhead at the end of FR-9737-112 (roughly 3,650 ft). At about 0.5 mile, bear left onto signed Trail #1391 (Beverly Turnpike/Beverly Creek Trail) — do not miss this junction, as a wrong-fork error onto the Bean Creek Trail is a commonly reported mistake. Continue to roughly 3.1 miles and turn right onto Trail #1226.1 (Fourth Creek Trail), climbing to Fourth Creek Pass at about 3.6 miles (roughly 5,900-6,000 ft), which opens up the first real views of Argonaut, Colchuck, and Dragontail. From the pass, descend the well-maintained trail on the far side to the south shore of Ingalls Creek at about 6 miles (roughly 4,200-4,250 ft); ford the creek (wading or a footlog depending on the season/year) to reach flat camping at the Fourth Creek/Ingalls Creek confluence. From camp, leave the Ingalls Creek Trail and climb generally north into the gentle, heather-and-slab Porcupine Creek drainage on Argonaut's south side, working up open basin terrain toward the broad saddle between Argonaut and Colchuck (the Argonaut-Colchuck col, about 7,700 ft), which most parties use to access the upper East Ridge. From the basin/col area, angle up snow or blocky rock to a notch on the ridge crest just west of a distinctive lone gendarme — this notch is where the roped, belayed climbing on the East Ridge (6 pitches) begins. Hazards: the Ingalls Creek ford can be a real obstacle in early season or after rain; the basin approach involves loose talus and, in shoulder season, hard snow that may warrant an axe and crampons; this is a long, remote approach (partial day just to reach the base) so plan for a car-camp or bivy.
backups.descent_text: Descend by reversing the East Ridge: downclimb and scramble back through the gendarme and knife-edge sections to the notch just west of the lone gendarme where the roped climbing began. From the notch, parties either make two single-rope rappels or one longer double-rope rappel (two ropes tied together, or twin/half ropes) down steep snow to the glacier/snow slopes below rather than downclimbing the exposed step -- both are standard, established options, not just one. Anchors on this route are natural — slung horns, blocks, or small trees — supplemented by whatever tat/fixed slings a prior party left; there is no bolted station, so carry extra webcord and be ready to build or back up an anchor. Once down to the snow/talus below the notch, downclimb into the basin and reverse the long approach: back down through Porcupine Creek basin, re-ford Ingalls Creek, and climb back out over Fourth Creek Pass to the trailhead. Given the length of this descent, start it with a comfortable margin of daylight.
backups.bail: The ridge can be retreated from with rappels off horns and blocks at several points, giving a reasonable escape if weather turns, though the long walk out remains a constant.

pitch_detail.notes: From the Argonaut-Colchuck col (~7,700ft) gain the east ridge crest over low-angle blocks and broken granite steps, easing into the climb before the terrain steepens.
Surmount a compact, steeper granite tower via face moves and thin gear placements; this is the route's technical crux and the most sustained pitch on the ridge.
Weave over and around a series of towers along the crest, alternating short exposed steps with easier ledge traverses; belay from a horn where the ridge narrows.
Moderate climbing and scrambling up blocky granite toward the upper mountain, with route-finding between minor gendarmes rather than sustained difficulty.
Continue past another gendarme on the upper ridge, staying near the crest on exposed but moderate granite before the angle relents toward the summit spires.
Class 3-4 ridge traverse to the base of the summit block, finishing with a short nonexposed scramble past the block's small cave feature to the true summit.

No source supports needing doubled ropes for the standard summer ascent/descent.

approach_variants.name: Beverly Turnpike TH over Fourth Creek Pass to Porcupine Creek basin
approach_variants.notes:
Beverly Turnpike Trailhead at the end of FR-9737-112, around 3,650 ft. At about half a mile bear LEFT onto signed Trail #1391 (Beverly Turnpike / Beverly Creek). Taking the Bean Creek fork instead is the commonly reported error and costs a lot of the day.

At roughly 3.1 miles turn right onto Trail #1226.1 (Fourth Creek) and climb to Fourth Creek Pass at about 3.6 miles and 5,900-6,000 ft, which opens the first real view of Argonaut, Colchuck and Dragontail. Descend the far side to the south bank of Ingalls Creek at about six miles and 4,200-4,250 ft, and ford — wading or a footlog depending on the season. Flat camping at the Fourth Creek / Ingalls Creek confluence.

From there leave the Ingalls Creek Trail and climb north into the Porcupine Creek drainage on Argonaut's south side: gentle heather and slab, open basin travel, working up toward the broad saddle between Argonaut and Colchuck at about 7,700 ft. Porcupine Creek basin also holds bivy sites.

Be aware this whole Teanaway-side trail network has been under a Forest Service closure order following the 2025 Labor Mountain Fire — confirm current status with the Cle Elum Ranger District before planning on it.

Note this trailhead is OUTSIDE the Enchantment Permit Area lottery boundary: a free self-issue wilderness permit covers you, even for an overnight.
hazards: Wrong-fork error onto Bean Creek Trail near the start
Ingalls Creek ford is a genuine obstacle in early season or after rain
Loose talus in the basin; hard snow in shoulder season warranting axe and crampons
Long, remote approach — a partial day just to reach the base, so plan a car-camp or bivy
Teanaway-side trail closures following the 2025 Labor Mountain Fire — verify before committing
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The base of the roped climbing is a NOTCH on the ridge crest, and the feature that identifies it is a single conspicuous GENDARME standing alone on the ridge. The notch you want is immediately WEST of that lone gendarme. Not east of it, not the next notch along — west, with the gendarme on your east side as you stand in it.

Getting there: from the Porcupine Creek basin or the Argonaut-Colchuck col area at about 7,700 ft, angle up snow or blocky rock to gain the crest. The southeast ridge can be crossed lower at a notch around 6,750 ft, so a notch on its own does not tell you much — the gendarme does.

In cloud, work the crest until you meet a free-standing tower, then take the gap on its west side. If you are already on knife-edge ground with exposure, you have gone past the start and are on the route.

bivy.name: Ingalls Creek valley camps below the Sherpa and Argonaut south sides
bivy.notes: This is the base for the south side of both Argonaut and Sherpa, and it is what makes those peaks feasible as overnights rather than brutal single pushes. Two ways in. From Esmeralda you climb to Longs Pass at about 6,200 feet and drop roughly 1,400 feet to the valley, then walk east along the trail until you are under your peak; Sherpa's south basin is about a mile down, Argonaut's exit gully perhaps three. From the low trailhead off US 97 you walk in flat but far, upwards of ten miles to reach the same ground, which trades the pass for distance and suits a party with time. A third link comes over Fourth Creek from the Beverly Creek trailhead in the Teanaway and requires fording Ingalls Creek, which is genuinely dangerous in June. The valley is low and sheltered, so it is buggy through midsummer and warm at night, and the brush between the trail and the open slopes above is the real work of the approach. Sites are dispersed rather than built, so pick an existing one instead of clearing new ground. The elevation of the trail changes across the several miles covered here, so no single figure is given.
bivy.water: Ingalls Creek runs strongly all season and side streams come in from the north wall; the only dry stretch is the climb over Longs Pass, which carries no water at all in either direction
bivy.permit: Alpine Lakes Wilderness under the Cle Elum Ranger District, entirely OUTSIDE the Enchantment Permit Area. A free self-issued wilderness permit from the trailhead box covers day and overnight use, there is no lottery, no quota and no reservation. A Northwest Forest Pass or day fee is needed to park at Esmeralda; the low Ingalls Creek trailhead off US 97 has its own parking requirement. Campfires are restricted seasonally and are a poor idea in any case; the valley is dry and forested. Camp at least 200 feet from the creek.
bivy.capacity: Numerous flat, well-used sites strung along several miles of valley floor and its side creeks; there is no quota and no realistic crowding, so a party can nearly always find its own ground

bivy.name: Beverly and De Roux campgrounds and the North Fork Teanaway roadside camps
bivy.notes: This is what most parties on Ingalls Peak actually use, because all three Ingalls summits are comfortably a long day from the car and there is no reason to carry a camp. Sleeping on the road puts you at the Esmeralda trailhead in minutes rather than driving up from Cle Elum in the dark. The Ingalls group sits entirely OUTSIDE the Enchantment Permit Area, in the Cle Elum Ranger District, so the whole permit problem that dominates the Icicle Creek side simply does not exist here: a free self-issued slip at the trailhead, a parking pass, and you go. Access is by pavement to the end of Teanaway Road and then gravel Forest Road 9737 for the last several miles; the surface is rough enough to want patience in a low car, holds snow into early summer, and washboards badly by August. Beverly is roughly four miles up the gravel and De Roux about eight, with Esmeralda a mile beyond that. If you do want to sleep high for the South Ridge, the designated sites in Headlight Basin are the legal option and camping is prohibited at Ingalls Lake itself; expect the goats there, which are bold, unbothered by people and interested in anything salty, so relieve yourself well away from camp and do not leave sweaty gear out.
bivy.water: No potable water at either campground, so bring what you need. The North Fork Teanaway River runs alongside and is easy to filter from.
bivy.permit: No wilderness permit at all, and nothing to do with the Enchantment lottery. Both campgrounds charge a modest per-night fee paid on site. Roadside dispersed camping is legal on National Forest ground along Forest Road 9737 but is NOT permitted inside the Teanaway Community Forest lower down the valley, where camping is confined to its designated campgrounds. Fire restrictions are common here from midsummer and are taken seriously; this valley is dry and burns. A Northwest Forest Pass is required to park at Esmeralda the next morning.
bivy.capacity: Beverly holds around fourteen small tent sites; De Roux is smaller still. Both are first come, first served with no reservations. Dispersed pullouts along the road hold many more parties informally.

backups.overview: Hozomeen Mountain is a dramatic, dark twin-summited peak rising directly from the east shore of Ross Lake near the Canadian border in North Cascades National Park/Ross Lake National Recreation Area. The higher North Peak (~8,071-8,072 ft) and slightly lower South Peak (8,003 ft) are built of Hozomeen chert, a hard but badly fractured bedded rock that gives the mountain its dark color and its reputation for notoriously loose, rotten climbing. The South Peak's nearly 1,000-foot near-vertical face (average angle ~42.6°) is often cited as the steepest in Washington. First ascents: North Peak, Sept 6 1904 (Sledge Tatum & George Loudon Jr., via the northeast); South Peak, May 30 1947 by Fred Beckey and five companions via the Southwest Route. The Southeast/South Face line described here is regarded as the least committing of the three known lines to the South Peak's summit, in contrast to the harder Southeast Buttress (Grade III, 5.6, FA 1988 by Adams/Goodman/Johnson/Petroske) and North Face (IV+ 5.9, FA 2019 by Rolf Larson & partner).
backups.beta: The Southeast Face offers a third-class approach to the summit, though grading varies by route variant and seasonal conditions. Most parties traverse the northeast ridge where it transitions to mixed terrain. Previous climbing experience on exposed, loose rock is essential.
backups.turnaround: Turn around if: conditions deteriorate to poor visibility, weather shows threatening signs (darkening clouds, lightning), party is moving slower than planned indicating fatigue, or snow/ice conditions require ongoing step-kicking above 7,500 ft. Allow at least 4 hours descent time and establish a firm turn-around time before committing to upper terrain.
backups.face: South Peak (8,003 ft - the lower of Hozomeen's two main summits)
backups.permit: North Cascades NP complex: no permit for day climbs; all overnight backcountry stays require a backcountry permit (reserve on Recreation.gov or walk-up at the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center).
backups.comms: No cell phone reception at Hozomeen Mountain or surrounding backcountry. Satellite communication (Garmin InReach, SPOT beacon) recommended for emergency contact. Remote location near Canadian border adds communication/evacuation delays.
backups.descent: Reverse the face; several fixed rappel bolts/anchors near the summit headwall and finishing chimney have been placed by past parties (per a 2019 ascent report), supplementing rappels off slung blocks or natural anchors where bolts aren't present. Do not blindly trust fixed gear on this rock — carry cord/webbing to back up or replace tat, and expect loose ledges and choss on the way down.

backups.pro_needs: Pro and slings for the low-fifth steps and to build/back up rappel anchors on questionable rock.
backups.approach: Because there is no public road to Hozomeen from the US side, the drive-in (SR-20 to Ross Lake Resort, then the resort's water taxi ~24 miles north up Ross Lake) drops you at the Hozomeen Ranger Station/Campground at the lake's head, around 1,650 ft — treat everything below as the hike from there. From the campground, pick up the maintained Hozomeen Lake Trail, which climbs gently through open, lush forest along the east side of Ross Lake toward Hozomeen Lake; trip reports differ on the exact length before you leave the tread (roughly 1.5 to 4 trail-miles depending on where you cut off), so budget for the full distance. Leave the maintained trail around 2,400 ft near Hozomeen Lake's outlet and begin ascending cross-country, following the creek/drainage east into the basin below the peak's south side. Expect a genuinely bad brush section here — a dense patch of devil's club right at the creek crossing, plus heavy deadfall and blowdown starting around 3,800 ft that slows travel to a crawl in spots. Water is reliable at the Hozomeen Creek crossing (~2,400-2,600 ft) and again in the basin around 5,000 ft; fill up at one of these, since the route above is dry. Near 5,000 ft the drainage narrows into a boulder-choked gully with a bottleneck of large chockstones; above that, tedious red scree and heather lead past a striking slab wall around 5,800 ft and a steepening final push to a broad saddle/basin around 6,800 ft, which is the standard high camp (flat, tent-sized sites, but small — good for one or two). From camp, gain the final 1,000-1,200 ft on slabs and connecting gullies to reach the base of the southeast face/ridge proper. Given the ~19 km round-trip distance and roughly 6,400+ ft of total gain from lake level, this is realistically an overnight approach for most parties (camp at ~4,900-6,800 ft) rather than a single continuous car-to-summit push; a few strong parties have done it in a very long day.
backups.descent_text: Descent reverses the southeast face/ridge — there's no separate walk-off, since Hozomeen drops steeply on essentially every side. The crux of the descent is a short, exposed step down a Class 5.6 bulge just below the summit ridge; some parties downclimb it, most rappel it given the exposure. Below that, a roughly 50-foot rappel gets you down a Class 5.0 ramp, and from there two further double-rope-length rappels (i.e., a 60m rope doubled, or twin-rope technique) lower you cleanly onto a snow patch/basin beneath the face — call it 3 rappels total as the typical count, though some parties report doing the lower section as one longer double-rope rappel instead of two, so bring a 60m rope and be ready for 3-4 rope-lengths depending on exact line and snow coverage. Anchors are mixed and not fully bolted: parties mention both fixed slings/webbing around blocks and horns and at least one bolted anchor near the crux/overhang, so treat any fixed tat as suspect, back it up, and carry a few extra slings/cord in case you need to build or replace an anchor. Below the rappels, downclimb loose scree and talus and reverse the approach gully back down to the ~6,800 ft saddle or camp — past parties describe this stretch as slow going (clean slabs mixed with steep dirt, shifting boulders, and loose rubble), with summit-to-camp times of roughly 3-6.5+ hours reported, so plan your day accordingly and expect to finish by headlamp if you start late.
backups.bail: Rappel from slung blocks; carry extra slings since fixed anchors are unreliable.

itinerary.cal: Access is via Ross Lake Resort's water taxi (SR-20 to Ross Dam, then boat up-lake to the Lightning Creek/Hozomeen area) since the historic Silver-Skagit Road border crossing from Hope, BC has been closed to both vehicle and foot traffic since the COVID-19 pandemic and remains closed as of 2026; best attempted mid-July through September once the west basin snow/water sources are known.

days.note: An easy 1.5-mile forest walk from the Hozomeen Lake trailhead gives way to a rougher off-trail push: crossing Hozomeen Creek, fighting devil's club and windfall, then climbing red scree and heather into the west basin below a broad slab wall. Most parties reach the 6,800 ft saddle camp by mid-afternoon, drop the overnight gear, and — if weather and energy allow — continue straight up for the summit the same day, returning to camp before dark. The final headwall below the summit is a short, exposed 5.6 step; bring a rope and rack a few pieces plus a sling for the fixed rap anchors used by past parties.

road.name: SR-20 (North Cascades Highway) to Ross Lake Resort; Silver Skagit Road from Hope, BC (closed at the border since 2020)
road.status: SR-20 is open seasonally and closes for winter avalanche danger (recent closures have run roughly early December through spring) between the Ross Dam trailhead and Silver Star Gate — check WSDOT/NPS road conditions before driving. The Silver Skagit Road has been closed at km 6 for wildfire since 24 July 2026, with no end date given in the B.C. Ministry of Transportation and Transit closure notice last updated 24 September 2026, and the border crossing into Hozomeen has been closed to travelers since 2020.
road.driveNote: Drive SR-20 to Ross Lake Resort (near Diablo/Ross Dam) and arrange the resort's water taxi (206-486-3751) to shuttle you the length of Ross Lake to the Hozomeen/Lightning Creek area, or hike in via the ~31-mile East Bank Trail from the SR-20 trailhead at milepost 138.
road.seasonalGate: Hozomeen Campground on the US side is open roughly late May through October; road passability should be checked directly before a trip.

climate.typical: Cool, wet North Cascades climate; snow can linger in upper gullies and on the face into July in heavy-snowpack years. Reliable, mostly snow-free rock conditions typically run mid-July through September.

bySeason.fall: Climbing season shortens rapidly after early September; early-season cold fronts and snow can hit the high ridge.
bySeason.spring: Approach trails and gullies are often still snow-covered/avalanche-prone into June, and Ross Lake Resort's water-taxi season may not yet be running.
bySeason.summer: Best climbing window (Jul-Sep); water sources above roughly 5,000-6,800 ft dry up by late summer, so time trips or cache water accordingly.
bySeason.winter: Effectively inaccessible — SR-20 is closed and Ross Lake Resort facilities are shut down.

emergency.notes: No cell phone reception at Ross Lake or Hozomeen; carry a satellite communicator/PLB. Given the multi-hour boat and/or long trail approach, rescue typically requires an NPS or county SAR helicopter.
emergency.rangerStation: North Cascades National Park - Wilderness Information Center (Marblemount) / Ross Lake NRA
emergency.nearestHospital: PeaceHealth United General Medical Center, Sedro-Woolley, WA (~65 mi via SR-20) — a small facility; serious trauma cases are typically flown out given the remote, boat/trail-only access to this peak.

crowds.peakTraffic: rarely climbed; no identifiable 'peak' traffic window - even the popular Mountaineers-documented routes on this peak see sparse annual ascents
crowds.estimatePerSeason: unknown - low-traffic; likely well under a dozen parties per season based on overall Hozomeen traffic patterns

fitnessSpec.hiking: Strong multi-day backpacking fitness for the remote Ross Lake/Hozomeen approach plus a steep, sustained climb to a high camp
fitnessSpec.packWeight: Overnight/multi-day pack (camp gear, food, water) for the approach, transitioning to a light summit pack for the pre-dawn face climb

partner_requirements.approachTime: Long, multi-day approach: boat/trail access to the Hozomeen area at the north end of Ross Lake, then a steep climb to a high camp below the face, with a pre-dawn start for the summit push
requiredSkills: confident movement on unprotected/loosely-protected Class 4-low 5th rock
routefinding on a complex, featureless face with unreliable anchors
loose/rotten rock management (testing holds, minimizing rockfall to partners)
remote self-rescue and sound turn-around judgment (no quick evacuation)
backcountry navigation on the approach from the Hozomeen area
partner_requirements.experienceLevel: Experienced alpine scrambler comfortable soloing/leading unprotected Class 4 to low 5th-class terrain on notoriously rotten rock, with solid judgment for routefinding on a complex, loose face far from help

July.reason: Primary climbing season begins; rock is as dry as it gets, though still loose, and lingering early-season snow patches on the approach are possible

August.reason: Most stable and driest month; best chance of avoiding wet rock, though afternoon thunderstorms remain a risk

September.reason: Still climbable and often stable, but early season snow and colder nights become more likely as the month progresses

weather.typical: Wetter north-end climate; the rock is hazardous when wet, so dry-weather windows are essential
weather.probability: Afternoon thunderstorms common in summer; rock remains loose even in dry conditions

seasonal_hazards.exposure: High consequence: extremely loose/rotten rock, sustained exposure, and unreliable anchors on unprotected Class 4/low 5th terrain, compounded by the remoteness of the objective (self-rescue only)

gaps: No confirmed first-ascent date/team specifically for this 'standard' Southeast/South Face line, as distinct from the documented 1988 Southeast Buttress FA and 1947 Southwest Route FA
Exact trailhead mileage varies by source depending on whether the (currently closed) north-end Silver Skagit Road or the long East Bank Trail from SR-20 is used
No public GPS track found for this route as of this research pass.

approach_logistics.trailheadDirection: From the Ross Dam Trailhead on SR-20 near milepost 134, down to Ross Lake and the water-taxi/trail network

backups.corrections: The listed route name/id ("Southeast Face (Standard)") does not correspond to any documented route on this summit. Every reputable source checked (Wikipedia, Mountaineers.org, SummitPost search results, multiple trip reports on trailcatjim.com, cascadeclimbers.com, and Cascade Alpine Guide references) describes the standard/easiest route on Hozomeen Mountain's North (main, 8,071-ft) summit as ascending the Northeast Ridge/Buttress from a col near 6,300 ft — first climbed 1904, class 4. A genuine "Southeast Buttress" route does exist in the American Alpine Club database (FA 1988, III 5.6, described as the least-committing of three known routes), but it is on the separate SOUTH Peak (8,003 ft) of Hozomeen, a distinct sub-summit roughly a mile away, not on the North Peak matched by this entry's coordinates. I have filled this entry's fields using the well-documented Northeast Ridge/Buttress standard-route data (setting aspect=NE, face=Northeast Buttress/Ridge accordingly) since that is what "the standard route" on this specific summit actually refers to in the literature; the routeName/routeId were kept exactly as given per instructions, but the aspect/face fields reflect the sourced reality rather than the "Southeast" label. Recommend the app data owner review whether this route entry should be renamed/re-pointed to the Northeast Buttress, or replaced with a distinct South Peak entry for the true Southeast Buttress line.

approach_variants.name: Water taxi up Ross Lake to the campground at the head of the lake
approach_variants.notes:
There is no public road to this end of the lake from the south. Drive to the trailhead near milepost 134, walk down to the resort, and take its water taxi north to the campground and ranger station at the head of the lake at about 1,650 ft. Everything below is measured from there.

From the campground pick up the maintained lake-side trail, which climbs gently through open lush forest toward Hozomeen Lake. Reports differ on how far along it you should stay - anywhere from a mile and a half to four miles depending on where the party cut off - so budget for the longer figure. Leave the tread around 2,400 ft near the lake's outlet and start up cross-country, following the drainage east into the basin under the peak's south side. There is a genuinely bad brush section here: devil's club right at the creek crossing, and heavy deadfall from about 3,800 ft that reduces travel to a crawl. Fill water at the creek crossing or again in the basin near 5,000 ft, because everything above is dry.
approach_variants.season: July through September, once the brush is passable and the upper gullies have melted out
hazards: a boat schedule that fixes both ends of the trip on a lake with no road out
devil's club at the creek crossing and heavy deadfall from about 3,800 ft
no water above the basin near 5,000 ft
a boulder-choked gully with chockstones to negotiate under a pack
loose, friable rock on the upper mountain
a tiny high camp that will not take a large party
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE LADDER OF LANDMARKS ABOVE THE BASIN IS WHAT FIXES YOUR POSITION, AND THEY COME IN ORDER. Near 5,000 ft the drainage narrows into a boulder-choked gully with a bottleneck of large chockstones - IF YOUR GULLY HAS NO CHOCKSTONE BOTTLENECK IN IT, YOU ARE IN THE WRONG DRAINAGE and should traverse rather than climb. Above the chockstones the ground turns to tedious red scree and heather. The next confirmation is a striking slab wall at about 5,800 ft, passed rather than climbed. Above it the angle steepens to a broad saddle and basin near 6,800 ft with small flat tent-sized sites - the standard high camp, good for one or two tents and no more.

FROM CAMP THE BASE OF THE ROUTE IS ANOTHER THOUSAND FEET OR SO ABOVE, GAINED ON SLABS AND CONNECTING GULLIES. You are looking for the point where the slabs run out against the face and the ridge proper takes over.

CHECK WHICH SUMMIT IS ABOVE YOU. This route is on the SOUTH peak, which is the lower of the two main summits. If the tower above you is the higher, broader one and the other summit lies to the SOUTH of you, you have drifted north into the wrong cirque and are under the north peak.

AND CHECK THAT YOU LEFT THE TRAIL AT ALL. The maintained tread is graded and obvious; the moment you are on it with easy walking under your feet, you are not on the approach any more. The departure is at a creek, at a lake outlet, not at a sign.

approach_variants.name: By road from the north to the ranger station, subject to the border gate
approach_variants.notes:
The campground and ranger station at the head of the lake can also be reached by driving a long gravel road south from the north side of the international boundary. That crossing has been closed to both vehicles and foot traffic, so this variant may simply not exist in the season you are planning for - confirm the gate's status before building a trip on it, because there is no way to discover it is shut except by arriving.

If it is open, the walk from the campground is identical to the boat variant: the maintained lake-side trail toward Hozomeen Lake, then off-trail at the outlet near 2,400 ft.
approach_variants.season: July through September, and only if the boundary is open
hazards: a border gate that has been closed to vehicles and to walkers
a long gravel drive with no services at the end
the same devil's club, deadfall and dry upper slopes
loose rock and a small high camp
approach_variants.baseFinding:
ARRIVAL CHANGES, THE APPROACH DOES NOT. From the campground at about 1,650 ft the sequence is the same: maintained trail to the vicinity of Hozomeen Lake's outlet near 2,400 ft, then cross Hozomeen Creek and follow the drainage east into the south basin.

THE MARKERS ARE THE SAME LADDER, IN THE SAME ORDER: a boulder-choked gully with a bottleneck of large chockstones near 5,000 ft, red scree and heather above it, a striking slab wall at about 5,800 ft, and then a broad saddle and basin at about 6,800 ft with a few small flat tent sites. A drainage with no chockstone bottleneck is the wrong drainage.

THE SUMMIT TEST STILL APPLIES. This route is on the SOUTH peak, the lower of the two. If the higher, broader summit is directly above you and the other one lies south, you are under the north peak instead.

approach_variants.name: From the Lightning Creek landing on the lake's east shore, past Willow Lake
approach_variants.notes: A boat landing further down the east shore of the lake gives onto the east-bank trail system, which runs north past Willow Lake. Parties have used this to reach the south and south-east sides of the massif on foot rather than starting from the campground at the head of the lake. It is the longer walk of the two boat options and it approaches the peak from the south-east rather than from the west, so it suits parties heading for the south-east side of the south peak more than it suits the standard line.
hazards: a much longer walk than the head-of-lake landing
timber, avalanche debris and a ravine crossing with no tread
steep dirt and brush below the shoulder
no water between Willow Lake and the basin
cliff bands that must be bypassed in poor visibility
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE DEPARTURE FROM THE TRAIL IS JUST BEYOND WILLOW LAKE, AND THE LAKE IS THE MARKER. It is the last reliable water; everything above is dry until the basin, so this is where you fill.

FROM THERE THE GROUND IS THE TEST RATHER THAN ANY TREAD: timber and avalanche debris first, then a ravine to cross, then steep dirt and brush climbing to open timber on the broad shoulder south of the peak. Reaching MEADOWS near 5,000 ft is the sign the worst of the brush is behind you.

ABOVE THE MEADOWS THE CLIFF BANDS ARE BYPASSED, NOT CLIMBED. If you are forced onto rock that wants a rope, traverse and look for the way round rather than committing to it - the way through here is a walking line, not a climbing one.

THE ARRIVAL IS A SADDLE AT ABOUT 6,200 FT DIRECTLY BENEATH THE BUTTRESS on the peak's south-east side, with no water on it. IF YOU HAVE ARRIVED SOMEWHERE WITH RUNNING WATER, YOU ARE NOT THERE YET. From that saddle the standard south-east face and the south-east buttress lines are both above you, so identify which feature you are under before starting up.

bivy.name: Improvised bivouacs in the western basin between the peaks
bivy.notes: The mountain is two rock summits above a basin, and the approach to that basin from the lake is the crux of the whole trip for most parties: a slow grind through blowdown and heavy brush with no path, on which fifteen miles and seven thousand feet of gain and loss is a fair reckoning for the round trip. Strong parties do go car to car, and parties often describe regretting that decision around hour twelve. Sleeping up here shortens the summit day considerably, at the cost of hauling water up a slope with almost none on it and sleeping on ground that is not flat. There is a second line from the road along the cleared border swath running east from near the ranger station, which is shorter and is described by people who have used it as more unpleasant than the lake approach rather than less. Both are late-summer propositions: snow lingers in the basin, and the brush is at its worst when it is wet.
bivy.water: This is the hard part and worth planning around. The one stream in the basin runs in a channel that deepens into a slot as you climb, and parties have found it reachable at a single awkward spot at around four thousand feet and nowhere above that. Fill everything you are carrying when you can get to water, because you may not get another chance before the ground goes flat enough to sleep on.
bivy.permit: National Park Service backcountry permit for the Hozomeen cross-country zone, which allows a maximum party of six and a maximum of three parties on any night. It is a walk-up zone rather than a reservable one, so the permit is collected in person, in practice at Marblemount. Cross-country camping legally begins a mile from any designated camp and half a mile from any trail, out of sight of both, and only on snow, rock or bare ground — never in meadow and never within a hundred feet of water. NO FIRES in the zone. Waste goes in a cathole, or is carried out where the ground will not take one.
bivy.capacity: No established site and no site count. Parties have reported scratching out a few rough platforms among scattered boulders on a steep forested slope, enough for one small party sleeping poorly. THERE IS NO CAMP HERE — this is where people stop because they have run out of daylight, not somewhere anyone chose.

bivy.name: Hozomeen Campground, north end of Ross Lake
bivy.notes: This is the roadhead for every route on the mountain and the only developed camping anywhere near it. It sits in deep forest on flat ground by the lake, with vault toilets, boat ramps and no trash service, so everything you bring comes out with you. There is no cell coverage and the nearest supplies are hours away in either country. The season runs roughly late May into October, bounded at the front by snow on the gravel road and at the back by the road being left unmaintained. The other way in is by water: a boat from the resort at the south end will run parties the length of the lake, taking up to six people with packs on a chartered trip that is booked and paid in advance. That is expensive and inflexible but it does not involve a border at all, which through several recent seasons has made it the only way anybody got here. In summer 2026 a lightning fire on the border grew to many thousands of acres immediately east of the mountain, crossed into Canada, and closed the entire Hozomeen area including the docks, the campground and the lake north of Silver Creek. Treat access to this peak as something to verify from scratch each season rather than as a fixed thing.
bivy.water: Seasonal potable water is provided while the campground is staffed. Outside that window, and any time the system is off, the lake and the creeks are the supply and need treating.
bivy.permit: National Park Service, Ross Lake NRA. No fee and no reservation for the campground itself, and no backcountry permit to sleep here — but one is required the moment you walk in to the lake camps or up onto the mountain. THE BORDER IS THE COMPLICATION. The only road access is a long gravel road running south from the Trans-Canada Highway near Hope, British Columbia, and it crosses into the United States at a point with no staffed port of entry. The gate on the American side has been closed to vehicle traffic from Canada for several years, and at times foot traffic across the line has been prohibited as well. A party driving down from Canada is entering the United States, so it needs the documents for that regardless of whether anyone is there to check; the practical position has been that you cannot legally drive through, and that a normal port of entry plus the boat is the way in. Confirm the current gate status with the park and with the border agency before committing to the road, because the answer has changed more than once.
bivy.capacity: Around 75 sites across two loops, all first-come and first-served with no reservations taken. The Upper Loop has been closed for hazard trees, which removes a good share of that number and also happens to be where the lake trail starts, so check what is actually open before counting on a spot.

bivy.name: Hozomeen Lake camp
bivy.notes: Something under four miles in from the campground's upper loop on an established trail, this is the obvious first night for anyone who wants to start the climb from higher than the road. It is a genuinely pleasant forested lake sitting directly beneath the mountain, and it is the better of the two lake camps by some distance. The climbing route leaves from here: parties work around the eastern shore and then angle up into the basin between the peaks, and that is where the day stops being a hike. Expect heavy deadfall and thick brush from the moment you leave the trail. The loon closure and the fire closures between them have shut this camp for large parts of recent seasons, so confirm it is open before building an itinerary on it.
bivy.water: The lake is right there and is the supply. It is standing water in a shallow forested basin, so filter or treat rather than drinking it as found.
bivy.permit: National Park Service backcountry permit required, obtained at the Marblemount wilderness office or through the park's issuing system. A SEASONAL CLOSURE APPLIES: the lake is closed to entry and to camping from the first of April through the end of May to protect nesting loons, which rules out the early-season window entirely. Fires and food storage are governed by the permit; a canister is the sensible choice here whatever the minimum requirement says.
bivy.capacity: A small designated backcountry camp at the lake, a few sites with a privy and food storage. Sites are assigned by night on the permit, so a walk-up can be turned away if the nights you want are taken.

backups.name: West Ridge / Southwest Gully
gear: ice axe (needed for the trail's north side and approach gullies into early-mid July)
crampons (the steep snowfield traverse below Kitling Peak can hold hard snow well into summer)
30m rope or a few slings if you prefer to rappel the crux chockstone in the summit gully (a fixed sling has been reported there)
hazards: loose, blocky rock along the ridge crest and summit gullies — rockfall risk to any party below
steep, hard snow in the approach gullies and on the Ragged Ridge traverse below Kitling Peak, often lingering into July
exposed Class 4 traverse around the north side of a false summit block just below the true summit
complex, cliffy gully/rib maze on the final summit pyramid — parties repeatedly report getting cliffed out without a GPX track or route photos
long, remote, very exposed ridge traverse with few bail options and high exposure to afternoon thunderstorms
backups.overview: Mesahchie Peak (8,795 ft) is the highest of four Bulger List summits on Ragged Ridge, 0.25 mi east of Katsuk Peak, between the Fisher Creek and Thunder Creek drainages in North Cascades National Park. First climbed in 1966. It's often cited as one of the hardest non-technical Bulgers on the list: the standard lines need no rope or glacier travel, but loose, blocky rock, a confusing gully/rib maze on the summit pyramid, and a long, exposed cross-country traverse of the Ragged Ridge crest from Easy Pass make route-finding and scrambling skill the real crux. Trip reports commonly note 'there's nothing easy about Easy Pass.'
backups.beta: Grade: Class 3/4 scramble on rocky terrain. Route description: From Mesahchie Col, cross talus to base of first obvious gully leading up west ridge. Initial section steep class 3/4 at bottom, broadens into gentler gully passing cairns. At 8,100 ft, descend 100 feet to enter south-side Class 3 gully with beige rock. Climb gully until it steepens, locate notch on left side, climb Class 4 deep cut traverse into second gully leading to ridge crest. Hazards: Extremely loose rock (every handhold requires testing), narrow ridge with significant exposure at summit. Required skills: Rock scrambling Class 3/4, exposure comfort. First ascent: 1966. Peak elevation: 8,795 feet (2,681 m), highest in Ragged Ridge.
backups.permit: North Cascades NP complex: no permit for day climbs; all overnight backcountry stays require a backcountry permit (reserve on Recreation.gov or walk-up at the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center).
backups.descent: From the summit, reverse the ascending gully/rib system to the ~8,050 ft ridge shoulder below the summit pyramid, downclimbing the crux Class 4 chockstone gully (a fixed rappel sling has been reported at this spot for parties who prefer to rappel it) and re-crossing the exposed traverse around the north side of the false summit block. Many parties avoid reversing the same terrain by ascending one ridge (e.g., the East Ridge) and descending the other (West Ridge/Southwest Gully), looping back down through forest to the Fisher Creek Trail before returning to Easy Pass. Watch for lingering steep, hard snow in the descent gullies, especially before August.
obj_haz: rockfall from loose blocky terrain on the ridge and summit gullies
sun-softened or hard-frozen snow on the approach traverse and gullies depending on time of day/season
afternoon thunderstorm exposure on the long, open ridge crest with few retreat options

waypoints.name: Easy Pass / Fisher Creek Trailhead
waypoints.note: On SR-20 near milepost 151, ~10-car lot with pit toilet; Northwest Forest Pass required to park.
waypoints.directions: Park at the Easy Pass/Fisher Creek Trailhead on SR-20, a marked pullout near milepost 151 about five miles west of Rainy Pass at roughly 3,700 feet elevation. The lot holds about ten cars, has a pit toilet and no water, and a Northwest Forest Pass is required to park. Overnight camping requires a backcountry permit, reserved in advance through Recreation.gov or picked up as a walk-up at the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center.

waypoints.name: Easy Pass
waypoints.note: Trail crests the Forest Service/North Cascades NP boundary here; views of Mt. Logan and Fisher Peak before the trail switchbacks down into Fisher Basin.
waypoints.directions: The Easy Pass Trail climbs steadily through forest and then open meadow and talus, gaining about 2,800 ft over three and a half miles; a fit party takes an hour and a half to two hours. Streams are reliable lower down but there is none at the pass itself, so fill up before the last switchbacks.

waypoints.name: Fisher Camp
waypoints.note: Established backcountry camp (3 tent sites, privy) in the Fisher Creek valley with water from Fisher Creek just downhill; used as the jump-off point to leave the trail for Mesahchie's south side.
waypoints.directions: From the pass the trail switchbacks down the far side, losing roughly 1,400 ft over three miles into the Fisher Creek valley. Every foot of that has to be climbed again at the end of the trip — budget around six hours summit-to-car and do not judge the exit by how fast this descent goes.

waypoints.name: Off-trail turnoff above Fisher Camp
waypoints.note: Leave the maintained Fisher Creek Trail roughly a half-mile past Fisher Camp and head upslope along the stream draining Mesahchie's southeast/south basin.
waypoints.directions: Stay on the Fisher Creek Trail for roughly another half mile past the camp, continuing gently downstream, until you reach a grassy, flower-filled glade. Nothing marks the departure and the maintained trail carries on past it, so it is worth fixing on a track; this is the last built tread of the day.

waypoints.name: 8,050 ft ridge shoulder
waypoints.note: Flat spot on the ridge at the base of the summit pyramid where the south rib meets the southwest gully system; descend a few feet south to enter the climbing gully.
waypoints.directions: Head cross-country and uphill along the drainage above the trail. Around 6,500 ft the line crosses a waterfall on an easy bench — the last reliable water, and the one real hazard on the approach, since it is slick and worse after rain or with snow still around. Above it, work up a mix of scree, talus, grass benches and low-angle blocky rock, threading short cliff bands and steep heather to a shoulder near 6,700-6,800 ft with flat bivy ground, then up the ridge crest itself, where a few Class 4 moves are needed to get established, onto gentler but loose cairned terrain. Everything above Fisher Creek is unmarked and parties do get cliffed out on this flank, so carry a GPX track or route photos rather than working from a description.

waypoints.name: Chockstone notch (crux gully)
waypoints.note: Rap-sling and cairn-marked gully narrows here; a Class 4 move past a chockstone in a notch gains the final summit ridge — very loose rock, test every hold.
waypoints.directions: Drop south off the shoulder to enter the first obvious gully on the southwest side, identifiable by its beige rock. It is steep Class 3-4 where it starts, then broadens and eases once a string of cairns appears. Follow it up until it steepens again and look left for the notch.

waypoints.name: Summit ridge crest
waypoints.note: Narrow crest with a series of small false points leading to the true summit; exposed scrambling on both sides.
waypoints.directions: The Class 4 move past the chockstone leads into a deep-cut traverse and a second gully, which runs up to the crest. The rock through here is genuinely rotten — test every hold, and keep the party out from under each other, because anything knocked loose funnels straight down the gully.

waypoints.name: Mesahchie Peak
waypoints.note: True summit of Ragged Ridge's highest point; panoramic views of Mt. Logan, Goode, and the Fisher Creek/Thunder Creek drainages.
waypoints.directions: Follow the crest over a series of small false points. One of them is turned by an exposed Class 4 traverse around its north side, the most committing move on the route; confirm the holds and your retreat before starting across. Past it the ridge is moderate but narrow, dropping away on both sides, to the top.

pro_tips: A fixed rappel sling and a large cairn mark the top of the crux chockstone gully — a useful way-finding checkpoint on both ascent and descent.
Many parties ascend one ridge (commonly the East Ridge) and descend the other (West Ridge/Southwest Gully) to make a loop back to the Fisher Creek Trail instead of reversing the same terrain.
Katsuk Peak is only 0.25 mi west of the summit and is frequently tagged on the same trip.
watch_out: The summit pyramid's gully/rib network is genuinely confusing — several parties have gotten cliffed out; carry route photos or a GPX track rather than relying on the general description.
The false-summit Class 4 traverse around the north side is 'wildly exposed' per multiple trip reports — don't commit without confirming the holds and turnaround options.
Hard, steep snow below Kitling Peak on the ridge traverse can persist into July even in an average year.
backups.pro_needs: Generally unroped scramble; a short rope and minimal protection useful for the exposed class 4 step in marginal conditions.
backups.approach: Start at the Easy Pass/Fisher Creek Trailhead on SR-20 (marked pullout near milepost 151, about 5 miles west of Rainy Pass, elevation ~3,700 ft; room for roughly 10 cars, pit toilet, no water at the lot). Follow the Easy Pass Trail, which climbs steadily through forest and then open meadows/talus, gaining roughly 2,800 ft over about 3.6 miles to Easy Pass (~6,500 ft); budget 1.5-2 hours at a good pace. There are reliable streams along the lower trail but none right at the pass, so top off water before cresting. From Easy Pass, drop about 1,400-1,500 ft on the Fisher Creek Trail into the Fisher Creek valley, passing Fisher Camp (~5,100 ft) and continuing downstream roughly another half mile to a grassy, flower-filled glade below Mesahchie's west/southwest flank - this is the key junction where you leave the maintained trail. Head cross-country and uphill, aiming for the drainage that comes down off Mesahchie's basin; around 6,500 ft the route crosses a waterfall on an easy bench (last reliable water before the ridge, and the one real ford/hazard on the approach - can be slick and is worse early season or after rain). Above the crossing, ascend a mix of scree, talus, grass benches and low-angle blocky rock, with steep heather slopes and short cliff bands requiring some routefinding, to a shoulder around 6,700-6,800 ft below the west ridge - a common bivy/high-camp site with flat tent spots. From here, work up the ridge crest (some class 4 moves getting established) to gentler but loose, cairned terrain leading to a col with a good bivy site. From the col, cross talus to the base of the first obvious gully leading up the southwest/west ridge - steep class 3/4 at its bottom, then broadening and easing after a string of cairns - and follow it to the ridge crest, then the exposed but moderate ridgecrest to the summit. Trailhead to the col/high-camp shoulder typically takes 4-4.5 hours for a fit party; the whole approach is loose and unmarked above Fisher Creek, so GPS or a photo of the route is worth having. Total one-way distance/gain to the summit run around 12 km and 4,900 ft of the route's overall 24.1 km / 7,480 ft round trip.
backups.descent_text: Standard descent is to reverse the ascent line: downclimb the ridgecrest and southwest gully back to the col, cross the talus to the ~6,700 ft shoulder/bivy site, then pick back down through the cliff bands and heather slopes to the cross-country entry point near the waterfall crossing and back onto the Fisher Creek Trail, before climbing back over Easy Pass and dropping to the trailhead. There is no mandatory rappelling - this is a class 3-4 scramble route and most parties downclimb the entire way - but an old rap sling sits on the bench at the top of the class 4 chockstone gully, and parties uncomfortable downclimbing that chockstone step sometimes back it off with a single-rope rappel (one rope length, roughly 30-50 ft, off the existing tat/natural block anchor - bring your own rap gear and consider backing up old slings, as their age/condition is unknown) rather than downclimbing it. The heather and slab sections lower down get notably treacherous when wet (parties describe lichen/moss-covered rock and multiple slips/falls in rain), and the waterfall crossing and loose talus/scree throughout are the main ongoing hazards. Summit-to-trailhead descent time is typically around 6 hours for a fit party (about 2 hours summit to high camp, remainder back to the car).
backups.bail: Retreat down the ascent gully; no easier alternative descent.

itinerary.cal: Overnight camping on Ragged Ridge is inside North Cascades National Park (Stephen Mather Wilderness) and requires a backcountry permit (quota via recreation.gov or walk-up at the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center); the route is typically snow-free and most climbed July-September.

days.note: Hike the maintained Easy Pass Trail to the pass, then leave the trail for cross-country ridge travel west along the Ragged Ridge crest, sidehilling below Point 7,690, crossing the 7,450 ft saddle south of Kitling Peak, and scrambling over Cub Peak (Class 3) before dropping to a flat camp spot on Mesahchie's shoulder. Route-finding on loose rock and heather benches is the crux of the day, not the elevation gain.

access.fees: $10 per person plus a $6 fee for an overnight wilderness permit (youth 15 and under free); a Northwest Forest Pass or America the Beautiful interagency pass is separately required for trailhead parking on SR-20.
access.notes: 60% of sites (Boston Basin/Eldorado/Sulphide Glacier/etc.) are reservable in advance via Recreation.gov (2026 lottery Mar 2–13); the remaining 40% are walk-up, obtained in person the day before at the Wilderness Information Center in Marblemount.
access.rules: Stay on trail, snow, or rock in the fragile subalpine terrain near the pass; no camping at Easy Pass itself; pets are prohibited throughout the national park; bear canisters are required (and loaned free) for some backcountry camps.
access.permit: Mandatory NPS wilderness permit for any overnight stay: $10 per person plus a $6 reservation fee, youth 15 and under free. Reserve in advance on Recreation.gov (watch the mandatory safety/rules video, then email noca_wilderness@nps.gov up to 3 days before the trip) or get a walk-up permit in person at the Wilderness Information Center in Marblemount (about 40% of permits are held for walk-ups). No camping is allowed at Easy Pass or in the surrounding meadows; nearest designated camps are Fisher Camp (~2 mi past the pass) and Cosho Camp (~6 mi along Fisher Creek). Day climbs with no overnight stay do not require a permit.
access.closures: SR-20 (North Cascades Highway) closes every winter due to avalanche hazard through the Rainy/Washington Pass corridor, typically from early December until sometime between late May and late June depending on snowpack (it opened as late as June 25 in 2026). The Easy Pass/Fisher Creek trailhead at milepost 151 is unreachable by car until the highway reopens.

climate.typical: Marine-influenced alpine climate with a heavy winter snowpack (the highway itself closes for avalanche hazard) and a short, generally reliable dry window from roughly late July through September. Afternoon thunderstorms and fast-moving weather are common on the exposed ridge crest in summer.

bySeason.fall: Larches turn gold in the high basins by late September/early October; days shorten and storm frequency increases.
bySeason.summer: Prime climbing window; expect residual snow on north-facing gullies and the Kitling Peak traverse into early-mid July, generally snow-free and driest by August.
bySeason.winter: SR-20 is gated closed and the approach is not feasible without extensive ski/snowshoe travel and serious avalanche exposure.

emergency.notes: This is a remote, multi-hour cross-country evacuation off the Ragged Ridge crest with unreliable cell coverage; a satellite communicator (inReach/SPOT) is strongly advised. Serious trauma cases from this area are typically airlifted (Airlift Northwest or military SAR) directly to Harborview Medical Center, Seattle's Level I trauma center, rather than driven out.
emergency.rangerStation: North Cascades National Park Wilderness Information Center, 7280 Ranger Station Road, Marblemount, WA 98267 (open mid-May to mid-October); (360) 854-7245.
emergency.nearestHospital: Skagit Valley Hospital (Level III trauma center), 300 Hospital Pkwy, Mount Vernon, WA — roughly 60-65 miles / 1.5+ hrs drive from the Easy Pass trailhead.
emergency.sheriffDispatch: 911; after-hours SAR coordination via Skagit County Sheriff (360) 336-9450, or NPS Communications Center after-hours (360) 873-4590 ext. 37.

crowds.peakTraffic: If any, late July through August once approach gullies clear of snow and Easy Pass trail is fully melted out; essentially empty on weekdays and in shoulder months
crowds.estimatePerSeason: Very low — likely well under 20 parties per season; no route-specific numeric logs found, this is a rough estimate based on remoteness and reported solitude

fitnessSpec.hiking: Strong, multi-day fitness: long off-trail approach over Easy Pass to a high camp (~6,700 ft) on Mesahchie's south shoulder before a full summit day on exposed terrain
fitnessSpec.packWeight: Overnight/multi-day pack (typically 2-3 day trip with camp at Fisher Camp or high camp) — expect roughly 30-40+ lb with camping gear, water, and scrambling kit

partner_requirements.approachTime: Multi-day approach: Easy Pass trail to Fisher Camp (~5,100 ft) then up to a high camp on Mesahchie's south shoulder (~6,700 ft); typically climbed as a 2-3 day trip rather than a single push

Comfort with sustained exposure on loose Class 3-4 rock
Basic snow travel / self-arrest for early-season snow lingering in approach gullies
Off-trail navigation (map/compass/GPS) — no maintained trail beyond Easy Pass
Rockfall awareness and party spacing in loose gullies
partner_requirements.experienceLevel: Experienced alpine scrambler comfortable with sustained, committing Class 3-4 terrain, loose/blocky rock, and cross-country route-finding on a remote unmaintained ridge — not appropriate for a scrambling novice's first outing.

seasonal_guidance.optimalWindow: Mid-July through September; late July through August is the most reliable stretch once approach gullies have shed snow

July.reason: Early-to-mid July gullies may still hold snow; conditions steadily improve and by late July this becomes a solid window.

June.reason: Approach basins are still snow-covered and in avalanche terrain this early in the season; not the intended window for this scramble.

August.reason: Prime scrambling window — gullies typically clear and weather is most stable, aside from afternoon thunderstorm risk.

September.reason: Still within the best-season; stable but shorter days and increasing chance of early-season storms.

weather.typical: Alpine North Cascades weather; rapid changes possible — the North Cascades are known for fast-moving fronts that can turn a clear morning into poor visibility on exposed ridge terrain.
weather.probability: Afternoon thunderstorms are a noted hazard here; combined with an early-dawn recommended start, this points to a strong pattern of building afternoon convection in summer that parties should beat by climbing early.

seasonal_hazards.exposure: High-consequence: sustained Class 3-4 climbing on loose, blocky rock along a committing ridge/gully system; a slip or rockfall from another party could cause a serious fall or strike a climber below.

avalanche.zone: No NWAC zone precisely covers Ragged Ridge/Easy Pass terrain; the nearest reference is the Washington Pass zone, and in any case NWAC issues forecasts only while SR-20 is open in winter/spring, so it has limited relevance to this route's actual (summer) climbing season

seasonal_hazards.crevasses: N/A - this route (West Ridge/Southwest Gully) stays on rock/gully terrain and does not cross glaciers; note the peak does have a small glacier/icefall on its north side (used by the separate Mesahchie Icefall Couloir route), which is not part of this route.

gaps: No single surveyed/official prominence figure was found; secondary sources disagree (2,235 ft per Wikipedia/NGS-derived data vs ~2,255 ft per a Peakbagger search snippet) — used the Wikipedia figure as internally consistent with the listed elevation.
Exact first-ascent date beyond the year (1966) and party names not established from available sources.
Approach/gain/distance stats are drawn from trip reports of a common East-Ridge-up/West-Ridge-down loop, not a single out-and-back on this specific route, so treat gain_ft/dist_km as approximate.
No trip reports newer than a few years old were reviewed, so current gully/snow conditions should be confirmed with a recent report before a trip.
