backups.rope_note: The West Ridge gully is steep Class 3/4 at its base, broadens above cairns, then a narrower branch has a Class 4 chockstone; near the ridge crest climbers cross an exposed slab before a crux ~150 ft Class 4 blocky headwall to the false summit. Some parties carry a short rope/handline for the chockstone and headwall crux.
rack: Short rope/handline for the crux chockstone and headwall

approach_variants.name: Easy Pass into Fisher Creek, then the south basin
approach_variants.notes: From the marked pullout on SR-20 near milepost 151 the Easy Pass Trail climbs steadily through forest and then open meadow and talus to the pass; streams are reliable low down and there is none at the pass, so fill up before the last switchbacks. From the pass the trail switchbacks down the far side into the Fisher Creek valley, past Fisher Camp, and continues gently downstream for roughly another half mile to a grassy, flower-filled glade. Nothing marks the departure and the maintained trail carries on past it, so it is worth fixing on a track — this is the last built tread of the day. Head cross-country and uphill along the drainage that comes down off the peak's basin. Around 6,500 ft the line crosses a waterfall on an easy bench, the last reliable water and the one real hazard low down, since it is slick and worse after rain. Above it, work up scree, talus, grass benches and low-angle blocky rock, threading short cliff bands and steep heather to a shoulder near 6,700 to 6,800 ft with flat bivy ground, then up the ridge crest itself, where a few Class 4 moves get you established, onto gentler but loose cairned terrain leading to the col.
approach_variants.season: Mid-July through September. Snow lingers in the approach gullies and on the ridge traverse into July, and the heather and slab lower down turn treacherous when wet.
hazards: genuinely rotten rock in the summit gullies — every hold needs testing and anything knocked loose funnels down the gully onto the party
the cliffy gully-and-rib maze on the summit pyramid, where parties repeatedly get cliffed out without a track or route photos
an exposed Class 4 traverse around the north side of a false summit block just below the top
the waterfall crossing at 6,500 ft, slick and worse after rain or with snow still around
lichen- and moss-covered rock lower down that becomes very slippery when wet
a long, exposed ridge with few bail options and real exposure to afternoon thunderstorms
approach_variants.baseFinding: THE ROCK CHANGES COLOUR AT THE START, AND THAT IS THE TEST. The base of the climbing is a flat spot on the ridge at about 8,050 ft where the south rib meets the gully system at the foot of the summit pyramid. From that flat spot you do not climb — you step DOWN a few feet to the south, on your left, to enter the first gully. The correct gully is unmistakably BEIGE, noticeably paler than the darker rock of the ridge you walked up, and it is steep Class 3 to 4 where it starts before broadening and easing once a string of cairns appears. Follow it until it steepens again and look left for a notch: a chockstone is jammed at the top of it and pulling past that chockstone is the Class 4 move that gains a deep-cut traverse into a second gully. Immediately above the chockstone you should arrive on a flat bench carrying an old rappel sling and a large cairn — if you have climbed a gully and found no bench, no sling and no cairn, you are in the wrong one. Two other ways to know you are wrong: if the gully rock is the same colour as the ridge, and if you started climbing upward from the flat spot instead of dropping a few feet south into it first.

climbing_route.label: West ridge crest to the col
climbing_route.notes: From the 6,700-6,800 ft shoulder, work up the ridge crest — some class 4 moves getting established — to gentler but loose, cairned terrain leading to a col with a good bivy site.

climbing_route.label: First gully on the southwest/west ridge
climbing_route.notes: From the col, cross talus to the base of the first obvious gully leading up the southwest/west ridge: steep class 3/4 at its bottom, then broadening and easing after a string of cairns; follow it to the ridge crest. Terrain here is loose and unmarked.

climbing_route.label: Ridgecrest to the summit
climbing_route.notes: The exposed but moderate ridgecrest leads to the summit.

bivy.name: Mesahchie basin, below the col
bivy.notes: This is the base for Mesahchie and the usual first night of any Ragged Ridge traverse. From Easy Pass the line goes cross-country west-northwest, sidehilling on heather and tiresome scree at around six thousand eight hundred feet for roughly three hours to reach the basin below Mesahchie Col. It is not a trail and it is not fast — talus, sidehill and sustained scrambling are the whole character of this ridge and parties consistently underestimate the traverse. From camp Mesahchie goes by its south side, Katsuk lies about half a mile further west along the crest by its south spur and east ridge, and Kimtah is beyond that again and is rarely worth a trip on its own. Note that camping is prohibited at Easy Pass itself and in the meadows around it, so this basin or the crest bivy is where the first legal ground is. All of it is inside the park, so leave the dog at home.
bivy.water: Running water in the basin, fed by snow above, and this is what recommends it over the ridge bivy higher up. It is the dependable choice late in a hot summer when the crest has dried out.
bivy.permit: NORTH CASCADES NATIONAL PARK backcountry permit required, without exception. Permits are reserved in advance through the national online reservation system and issued by park staff shortly before the trip, by email or in person at the wilderness desk in Marblemount, with a per-person recreation fee and a small booking fee on top. Camping is in a cross-country zone rather than at a named site, and an approved bear-resistant canister is required wherever there is nothing to hang food from, which up here is everywhere. No campfires; carry a stove.
bivy.capacity: Unimproved ground for a couple of small tents on benches in the basin under Mesahchie and Katsuk. Nothing is built here — no pads, no privy, no fire ring, and there should not be.

bivy.name: Easy Pass trailhead, SR 20
bivy.notes: This is the only practical trailhead for Mesahchie, Katsuk, Kimtah and Mount Arriva, and it is worth understanding what the walk in costs before committing to it. The trail climbs roughly three thousand feet in a little under four miles, gently through forest at first and then in steep switchbacks up a headwall of loose rock with real exposure to weather; the name is old optimism and nothing about it is easy under a climbing pack. Snow holds on the upper switchbacks and in the basin above into July in an ordinary year and later after a heavy winter, and that traverse is where parties turn around. There is a toilet at the lot and parties routinely sleep in the car here before a pre-dawn start. Dogs may come only as far as the pass, because the top of the pass is the national park boundary.
bivy.water: None at the lot. Granite Creek is crossed on a bridge a few minutes up the trail and is the last easy water low on the approach.
bivy.permit: Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass to park. No camping permit is needed on the forest side of the pass. THE MOMENT YOU CROSS THE PASS THE RULES CHANGE COMPLETELY — see the Ragged Ridge and Fisher Creek entries below.
bivy.capacity: A small lot with room for roughly ten cars, on a short spur off the highway between mileposts 151 and 152. It is genuinely small and can be full on a good weekend.

bivy.name: Fisher Camp, Fisher Creek basin
bivy.notes: Fisher Camp sits in the forested basin west of and well below Easy Pass, reached by carrying on over the pass and descending into Fisher Creek. It is the comfortable option and it is also the alternative approach to Kimtah that some parties prefer: rather than the long sidehill traverse along the south flank of Ragged Ridge, they drop into the basin, losing something like eighteen hundred feet, and then climb a more direct line straight back up to the crest. Whether that trade is worth it depends on snow on the traverse and on how much the party dislikes scree. Further down the valley the trail passes additional designated camps toward the Thunder Creek junction, which is how a Ragged Ridge trip can be finished as a through-hike rather than an out-and-back. The descent to this camp is real elevation that has to be regained on the way out, and it is the reason a summit-focused party stays high instead.
bivy.water: Fisher Creek, right at the camp, and it runs all season. This is the most reliable water anywhere on the Ragged Ridge side.
bivy.permit: North Cascades National Park backcountry permit required and reserved for this specific named site, not for a zone. Book in advance through the national online system and collect the permit from park staff shortly before the trip. Food must be stored properly; a canister is the simplest answer. No campfires, and no dogs anywhere beyond Easy Pass.
bivy.capacity: Three designated sites — two taking a single tent each and one that will hold about four. A privy is provided. Being a named camp rather than a zone, it is reserved specifically and can simply be full.

bivy.name: Ragged Ridge crest bivy, south of Mesahchie Col
bivy.notes: This is the higher and more committing of the two Ragged Ridge camps, about a mile west-northwest of Easy Pass. Two ways reach it: sidehill west at roughly six thousand eight hundred feet on heather and scree, or climb the grassy slope just past the pass to gain the crest near seven thousand two hundred feet and follow the ridge until the ground steepens toward the 7,690-foot point, where it turns technical. The reward is a start already on the ridge for a long traverse day toward Katsuk and Kimtah; the cost is wind, cold and the water problem. Mount Arriva goes the other way from the pass, southwest, so a party after Arriva alone gains nothing by coming up here. Pitch on gravel rather than on the heather, which is thin and slow to recover, and expect a party of more than two to be split across separate patches of ground.
bivy.water: SEASONAL AND OFTEN GONE. Snow patches supply it early and it is commonly dry by late summer, which is the one reason to prefer the basin below. Coming up here late in the year means carrying water or dropping into the basin to fetch it.
bivy.permit: North Cascades National Park backcountry permit required, reserved in advance and issued by park staff before the trip. Cross-country zone camping with an approved bear canister, and no campfires. There is no self-issue option anywhere on this side of the pass — the free trailhead-kiosk permits people are used to on the forest do not exist here.
bivy.capacity: A small high bivy on the south side of the crest, east of the 7,985-foot subpeak. Room for one or two parties on gravel and heather. Exposed, with no shelter of any kind.

backups.fa: Unknown (Glacier Peak was first climbed in June 1897 by a USGS party via the Sitkum Glacier)

Rope and harness for roped glacier travel — the Cool Glacier keeps open crevasses through the season per the published route description

backups.overview: The Disappointment Peak Cleaver is the standard southern approach to Glacier Peak, reached via the North Fork Sauk River Trail, White Pass, and Glacier Gap. From Glacier Gap (~7,250-7,300 ft), the route follows the broadening cleaver north; near ~8,500-8,600 ft climbers either scramble directly over Disappointment Peak — a sub-summit with only ~115 ft of prominence above Glacier Gap — on 4th-class terrain, or bypass it via a rising traverse under it onto the upper Gerdine and Cool glaciers to a col at ~9,100 ft, then continue up steepening snow to the summit.
backups.beta: Where the standard route leaves the cleaver around 8,500-8,600 ft for a rising traverse under Disappointment Peak onto the upper Gerdine and Cool glaciers, a variant instead continues directly up the nose of the cleaver on a climber's trail (when melted out), steepening into mostly 3rd/4th class terrain (with a few 5th-class moves) between about 8,500 ft and Disappointment Peak's 9,755 ft summit. From there, descend slightly to the saddle above the Cool Glacier to rejoin the standard route to Glacier Peak's summit. The variant's main appeal is avoiding most of the glacier travel and crevasse hazard, traded for sustained loose, rockfall-prone scrambling.
backups.turnaround: Turn around by early afternoon on summit day given the remote camp and long return.
backups.permit: Free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit at the trailhead; no quota. Northwest Forest Pass at many trailheads.
backups.comms: No reliable cell coverage; carry a satellite messenger.
backups.descent: Reverse the route to high camp and the long trail out.

backups.pro_needs: Glacier protection only — pickets for steeper snow and crevasse zones.
backups.best_season: Late June through August for snow-covered glaciers and a melted-out approach.
backups.approach: From the North Fork Sauk River Trailhead (2,050 ft, end of Sloan Creek Road/FR 49), the North Fork Sauk River Trail (#649) climbs gently through old-growth forest. At about 2.1 miles pass the Pilot Ridge Trail junction (an alternate/bailout route), and by roughly 3.5 miles reach a crossing of Red Creek — a seasonal ford that can be a genuine early-season obstacle. About 1.5 miles beyond that is Mackinaw Shelter, the last reliable flat camping and water before the climb steepens; many parties camp here or push on. Past the shelter the trail switchbacks steeply for about 3 miles, gaining roughly 2,000 ft to reach the Pacific Crest Trail at White Pass (~5,900–6,000 ft) — this junction is the standard high-camp area and the effective end of maintained trail. From White Pass, follow a climbers' path/use trail traversing north into the White Chuck Glacier/Glacier Gap basin toward the toe of the Cool Glacier (~7,000 ft). This traverse passes below Disappointment Peak's east face, a known rockfall corridor — helmets on, and stay climbers' right (i.e., higher/farther from the base of the peak) on the way in to minimize exposure to falling rock. Since the 2003 floods destroyed the shorter west-side (White Chuck) access, this North Fork Sauk approach has become the standard route to Glacier Peak, pushing round-trip mileage to roughly 34–35 miles — noticeably longer than the old approach.
backups.descent_text: No rappelling — this is a full glacier/snow walk-off, reversing the ascent line. From the summit, downclimb the Disappointment Peak Cleaver ridge back to the 9,600 ft col, then descend the Cool Glacier to the 9,100 ft col. Cross back beneath Disappointment Peak on the return traverse staying climbers' left (i.e., lower, farther from the peak) this time to reduce time exposed under active rockfall — trip reports specifically note ascending right/descending left as the safe pattern here. Crevasses on the Cool Glacier open up significantly by mid-to-late season, with reports of 'house-eating' cracks near the col and snow bridges that weaken through the summer — rope up and probe suspect bridges, and expect the safe line to shift as the season progresses. Continue down to White Pass and out the North Fork Sauk River Trail to the trailhead.
backups.bail: High camp at Glacier Gap is the bail point; retreat from the upper mountain returns you there, then the long walk out.

pitch_detail.notes: North Fork Sauk Trail to Mackinaw Shelter, then a steep 2,000 ft of switchbacks to the PCT at White Pass. A climbers' path traverses north past the White Chuck Glacier basin to Glacier Gap (about 7,250–7,300 ft), where the White Chuck and Suiattle glaciers meet and there is ample camping. The Red Creek ford can be a real early-season obstacle.

From Glacier Gap climb the ridge north, first on its left side, then moving right beneath Glacier Gap Peak, and regain the crest around 8,400 ft. The rock is loose throughout, so keep parties close together. Where the cleaver steepens, most parties put on crampons and helmets and step off the dirt onto snow.

Traverse right (northeast) onto the upper Suiattle Glacier and continue below the cliffs of Disappointment Peak to the upper Cool Glacier near 9,200 ft. The stretch under the cliffs, around 8,600 ft, is an active rockfall zone: cross it fast and without stopping, particularly on the way down once the snow softens. Rope up for the glacier once past it.

Climb the Cool Glacier westward to the col above Disappointment Peak at about 9,600 ft, passing medium to large crevasses that open wider as summer goes on. Alternative that avoids the glaciers: scramble over Disappointment Peak (9,755 ft) on 4th-class loose rock and drop about 150 ft to the same col. Most parties unrope at the col.

From the col follow the ridge north-northwest on a steep volcanic dirt path or snow, bearing up and left until an obvious moderate slope leads straight north to the summit ridge for the last 200–300 ft. That final slope is often firm snow near 35°, so keep the axe out; the sandy ridge is loose underfoot and sheds rock onto parties below.

approach_variants.name: North Fork Sauk River Trail #649 to White Pass and Glacier Gap
approach_variants.notes:
North Fork Sauk River trailhead at about 2,050 ft, off Sloan Creek Road (FR 49). The trail runs gently through old growth: the Pilot Ridge junction at roughly two miles, a crossing of Red Creek at about three and a half that can be a real obstacle early in the season, and Mackinaw Shelter about a mile and a half further — the last flat camping with easy water before the climb steepens.

Past the shelter the trail switchbacks hard for about three miles and two thousand feet to meet the Pacific Crest Trail; turn right and go a quarter mile to White Pass at about 5,900 ft. This is the standard high-camp area and the end of maintained trail.

From White Pass a use trail traverses north into the White Chuck Glacier basin. Skirt or cross the glacier and rise onto its north-east lobe to Glacier Gap at about 7,250 ft.

This has become the main way up Glacier Peak since the White Chuck trail on the west side washed out, and it makes for a round trip in the mid-thirties of miles — considerably longer than the historic approach.

approach_variants.baseFinding:
Glacier Gap is the reference point and it has a definition you can verify in cloud: it is the col where the White Chuck and the Suiattle glaciers MEET. If you are standing on a saddle with ice on only one side of you, it is not Glacier Gap.

Above the gap the cleaver begins as a gentle ridge and sharpens as it runs north. That gentleness is why parties overshoot the start — there is no abrupt step to tell you the route has begun. From here there are two choices, and they are genuinely different climbs: go directly over Disappointment Peak, which is fourth class, or skirt it by climbing the upper margins of the Gerdine and Cool glaciers.

The negative marker that matters most on this route is near the top. The first summit reached along the cleaver is Disappointment Peak, not Glacier Peak — if you have topped out and the true summit is still rising well above and beyond you across more ground, you are on Disappointment and have not finished.

One more, on the way in: the traverse from White Pass toward the Cool Glacier passes below Disappointment Peak's east face, which is a rockfall corridor. Helmets on, and stay higher and further out from the base of the peak rather than hugging it.

bivy.name: Glacier Gap
bivy.notes: PLANNED high camp and the standard staging point for the Cool Glacier and the cleaver. Plenty of established gravel sites with rock walls already built, which exist because the gap funnels wind — it is known for wind and for storms rolling through after dark, so use the walls and pitch low. Some sites are dry camps; the seep below camp is the dependable one and it is the last water on the route. The last mile and a half in is loose scree and boulders.

backups.overview: The Gerdine Ridge and Cool Glacier route approaches Glacier Peak from the southeast, typically via the White Pass and Glacier Gap. It is a popular alternative to the Sitkum, often combined with a scenic high traverse beneath the peak.
backups.beta: From Glacier Gap (7,300 ft), ascend northward, initially contouring the left slope below Glacier Gap Peak (7,739 ft), then regain the ridge and continue to about 8,400 ft. Traverse NE onto the upper Suiattle Glacier, then ascend the Cool Glacier westward until regaining the ridge at its top, finishing to the summit. An alternate avoids all glacier travel by climbing directly up the South Ridge to Disappointment Peak (9,755 ft) before descending slightly to the saddle above the Cool Glacier — useful for parties without full glacier gear or climbing very late season.

waypoints.note: Trail gains ~3,000 ft in the final stretch to this meadow junction with sweeping views of Glacier Peak; join the PCT here.
waypoints.directions: Beyond the old shelter site the trail turns into roughly three miles of switchbacks, gaining about 3,000 ft to the meadows at White Pass. Water is unreliable once you leave the river, so fill up before starting the climb. The PCT junction is at the top.

waypoints.name: Foam Creek Trail / ridge saddle crossing
waypoints.note: Leave the PCT on the Foam Creek climbers' path and cross the ridge saddle into the White Chuck Glacier basin.
waypoints.directions: From the PCT at White Pass, take the Foam Creek climbers' trail east for about two miles, then cross the ridge at a saddle on its north side near 6,600 ft. This saddle is the end of trail travel — beyond it the route is open basin and snow.

waypoints.name: White Chuck Glacier basin crossing
waypoints.note: Open glacial basin traverse trending NE toward Glacier Gap; rope up here as crevasses can be present even though the grade is gentle.
waypoints.directions: Drop north off the saddle into the open White Chuck Glacier basin and trend northeast across it. The grade is gentle, but it is glacier under the snow, so rope up before you start across rather than partway.

waypoints.name: Glacier Gap
waypoints.note: Large, popular camp area with many established sites on a broad gap; standard base camp for the Gerdine Ridge/Cool Glacier route.
waypoints.directions: Continue northeast across the basin, gaining a few hundred feet to the broad gap where the White Chuck and Suiattle glaciers meet. Established sites are spread across the gap, and it is the last flat ground before the summit push.

waypoints.name: Cool Glacier saddle (Gerdine-Cool col)
waypoints.note: Saddle between Disappointment Peak and Glacier Peak where the Gerdine Ridge route tops out onto the Cool Glacier for the final push.
waypoints.directions: Leave camp on crampons, losing a little height onto rocky Gerdine Ridge, then climb north, contouring the slope below Glacier Gap Peak before regaining the crest and following it to roughly 8,400 ft. The climber's track ends near a gendarme around 8,500 ft — rope up there, traverse northeast onto the Gerdine and upper Suiattle ice, and end-run one or two crevasses where it bends into the Cool Glacier. Keep moving on that traverse; the cliffs of Disappointment Peak above it shed rock. Finish by climbing west up the Cool Glacier to regain the ridge at the saddle.

waypoints.name: Glacier Peak summit
waypoints.note: True summit of Glacier Peak (Dakobed); broad volcanic summit with views across the North Cascades.
waypoints.directions: From the saddle the glacier travel is over. Rejoin the climber's trail and finish up one short, steep pitch of pumice and broken volcanic rock to the top — unroped class 2-3, with no rock gear needed.

approach_variants.name: North Fork Sauk to White Pass, then the Foam Creek high traverse
approach_variants.notes:
From the North Fork Sauk River trailhead at about 2,050 ft, take Trail #649 up the valley and then the steep switchbacks to the Pacific Crest Trail at White Pass, roughly nine miles in.

Rather than dropping into the basin, continue east on the Foam Creek trail for about two miles, cross a ridge saddle near 6,600 ft, and traverse the White Chuck Glacier basin trending north-east to Glacier Gap at about 7,250 ft — where the Suiattle and White Chuck glaciers meet, and the standard high camp.

Summit day from Glacier Gap is short in distance but has intermediate descent in it as well as gain: gentle snow above camp, then a climbers' track over volcanic scree onto the Gerdine and Cool glaciers.

crevasses on the Gerdine and Cool glaciers
loose volcanic scree on the connecting ground
long approach with no maintained trail above White Pass
approach_variants.baseFinding:
Glacier Gap is confirmed the same way as for the cleaver — it is the col where two glaciers meet, not a saddle with ice on one side only.

This route deliberately AVOIDS the fourth-class ground: the line skirts Disappointment Peak by staying on the upper edges of the Gerdine and then the Cool. So the test that you are on the right variation is that you are on snow and scree the whole way, working around the peak rather than over it. If you are scrambling rock and gaining a summit, you have drifted onto the direct line over Disappointment Peak.

On the Cool Glacier expect to end-run one or two crevasses before rejoining the climbers' track for the final steep pitch to the summit — that track, worn into scree and snow by traffic, is the most reliable confirmation you are on the standard line, so look for it rather than for a feature.

climbing_route.label: Gentle snow above Glacier Gap camp
climbing_route.notes: From the ~7,300 ft Glacier Gap camp head north, sidehilling first on the left slope and then on the right slope below Glacier Gap Peak (7,739 ft), then regain the ridge and follow it to about 8,400 ft. A short scramble of about 15 ft at the top of this section drops onto the glacier.

climbing_route.label: Volcanic scree onto the Gerdine and Cool glaciers
climbing_route.notes: Traverse northeast onto the upper Suiattle and Gerdine glacier ice, passing below and right of the cliffs of Disappointment Peak. Few crevasses, but rockfall off that face is frequent and can include very large blocks, worst after about 10 AM — keep a wide berth and do not stop beneath it. Late in the season a short stretch of bare ice appears.

climbing_route.label: Cool Glacier to the saddle
climbing_route.notes: At about 9,200 ft the ice bends sharply left onto the Cool Glacier; climb it westward to the saddle between Disappointment Peak and the main peak at the glacier's top. This is where the real crevasses are — small cracks at the bend, then snow bridges and crevasse hops that deteriorate fast in late summer — so stay roped.

climbing_route.label: Final steep pitch to the summit
climbing_route.notes: Follow the ridge north on the climbers' trail, up loose pumice and scree that slides back underfoot, to about 10,000 ft, then climb steep snow or loose rock for the last ~500 ft to the 10,541 ft summit, which sits on the west side of the top. Which surface you get depends on the season.

bivy.name: Glacier Gap
bivy.notes: This is the high camp for Glacier Peak by the Cool Glacier and Gerdine Ridge, and the single most-used climbing camp on the mountain. It sits at about 7,300 feet at the head of the basin, reached by crossing what is left of the White Chuck Glacier northeast from the White Pass area — and what is left is the point, because that glacier has retreated faster than almost anything else in the range and the crossing is now largely bare rock, pumice and meltwater ponds rather than ice. From camp the route works up the ridge to about 8,400 feet, traverses onto the upper Suiattle Glacier, gains the upper Cool Glacier around 9,200 feet and climbs it westward to regain the ridge for the summit. Summit day from here runs long by any measure and thirteen hours camp to camp is normal rather than slow. Being a gap it funnels wind, so build or use the rock walls. Most parties take three days from the North Fork Sauk road and a fourth is worth having for weather.
bivy.water: Meltwater streams off the surrounding snowfields, running through most of the climbing season but silty; late in a hot summer it can be reduced to a drip from the base of a snow patch, so scout it on arrival rather than at dinner time
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit. No fires — this is bare rock, pumice and alpine ground above treeline with no wood and nothing that recovers. Twelve-person party limit. Human waste needs carrying out or burying properly well away from the meltwater, which everybody camped here is drinking.
bivy.capacity: A large basin with many bivouac sites and rock-walled platforms — it takes a lot of parties without feeling crowded, and there is always room to build another windbreak

bivy.name: Mackinaw Shelter camp, North Fork Sauk
bivy.notes: This is the first night for a Glacier Peak climb by the Cool Glacier and Gerdine Ridge, which is the route most parties use now that the western approaches have gone. It sits about five flat miles up the North Fork Sauk trail through genuinely large old-growth, and the walk in is easy enough that a party arriving late in the day can still reach it. The shelter the camp is named for collapsed years ago and there is no roof here — treat the name as a map label rather than a promise. Camping here rather than pushing on matters because the next three miles gain three thousand feet in relentless switchbacks with no reliable water on them, so this is the place to drink, fill everything you carry, and start that climb cool. Coming out, most parties pass straight through. Access is the problem rather than the camp: the December 2025 storms damaged roads and trails across this side of the wilderness and reaching the North Fork Sauk trailhead at all should be confirmed before the drive, not assumed.
bivy.water: Excellent and year-round — the North Fork Sauk runs right past the camp, and this is the last dependable water before White Pass
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit, filled in and deposited at the trailhead box. Party size is capped at twelve, counting people and stock together. A Northwest Forest Pass or America the Beautiful pass covers parking at the road end. Fires are not banned outright at this elevation but summer forest-wide restrictions routinely prohibit all open flame from midsummer, so plan on a stove.
bivy.capacity: A handful of established sites in the trees on a river bench, comfortably two or three parties, and the only organised camping in the valley bottom

bivy.name: White Pass and the Foam Creek benches under White Mountain
bivy.notes: White Pass at about 5,900 feet is the second night for a Glacier Peak climb, or the first if a strong party pushes the whole eight and a half miles and three thousand feet from the road in one go. It is the point where the North Fork Sauk trail meets the long-distance crest trail and where the climbing approach turns east. From here a boot path runs east-northeast under the southeast side of White Mountain for a bit over a mile toward a high shoulder, then the Foam Creek path traverses on toward an eastern col at around 6,600 feet for the first view of the mountain. Parties who want to break the approach differently camp somewhere along that traverse rather than at the pass itself, which trades a sheltered established site for wind and a shorter summit day. It is exposed ground once you leave the pass, with nothing to hide behind in a thunderstorm, and the traverse is genuinely confusing in fog.
bivy.water: A small spring and snowmelt at the pass, dependable early but often down to a trickle by late season; the benches toward Foam Creek hold snowmelt into midsummer and then dry out
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit, twelve-person party limit. Northwest Forest Pass at the trailhead. Camp on the existing bare sites — this is fragile subalpine meadow that recovers slowly and is heavily used. Carry a stove; open flame is inappropriate here and is usually prohibited outright under summer restrictions.
bivy.capacity: Several established sites just south of the pass, plus scattered ground on the benches east of it; a popular crossroads with a long-distance trail running through it, so expect other parties in July and August
